analysis.one_liner: Makes illegal robocalling a criminal offense punishable by up to three years in prison and doubles fines for spoofed caller ID.
analysis.headline: The bill to make robocalling a jailable offense was referred to committee and never received a vote before the 117th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The DO NOT Call Act would make it a federal crime to knowingly break the ban on automated telemarketing calls and texts. First-time violators could face up to a year in prison, and repeat offenders, high-volume callers, and scams that cost victims $5,000 or more could face up to three years. It also doubles the fine for knowingly faking caller ID information to $20,000 [S2][S3]. The bill never advanced past its committee referral before the Congress ended [S1][S5].
analysis.who_benefits: If enacted, ordinary phone users would benefit: the bill targets the illegal automated calls and scam texts that bombard nearly every household, adding jail time for repeat and high-volume offenders and doubling the fine for faking caller ID to $20,000 [S2][S3]. Legitimate telemarketers who follow the rules are unaffected, since the penalties apply only to willful and knowing violations of the existing ban [S3].

how_it_helps.text: Makes intentional robocall violations a crime carrying up to one year in prison, and up to three years for repeat offenders, callers blasting over 100,000 calls in a day, or scams causing at least $5,000 in losses.
Doubles the fine for knowingly transmitting fake or misleading caller ID information from $10,000 to $20,000.

analysis.who_pays: The cost would fall on illegal robocallers and scam operators, who would face prison time and doubled spoofing fines [S2][S3]. Honest businesses bear essentially nothing, as penalties apply only to willful violations.

drawbacks.text: Criminal penalties require proving willful, knowing violations beyond a reasonable doubt, which may make convictions rare and the deterrent effect limited for hard-to-reach operations.
The bill only increases penalties under the existing statute; it does not add enforcement funding or new tools, so its practical impact depends entirely on whether prosecutors bring cases.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The upside is real but modest: robocall scams cost Americans billions a year, and criminal jail time plus doubled caller-ID fines could deter the worst operators [S2][S3]. The drawback is that criminal penalties mainly reach the individual scammers who get caught, while the volume of illegal robocalls is driven by networks, gateway providers, and overseas operations that may be hard to prosecute; enforcement capacity matters as much as new penalties. Even so, the costs are negligible for law-abiding callers, and the honest objection is not that the bill is harmful but that it was a narrow response to a large problem.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the Energy and Commerce Committee and its communications subcommittee, never got a hearing or a vote, and died when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Representative Deborah Ross introduced the bill on August 3, 2021, with four Republican cosponsors.
It was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee the day it was introduced, then to the Subcommittee on Communications and Technology the next day.
No further action was taken before the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023, so the bill expired without a vote.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Robocall and telemarketing scam operations, which faced no added criminal penalties; no one else gained.

for.name: Rep. David Kustoff

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to subcommittee and took no further action on it before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: A Democratic sponsor gathered four Republican cosponsors, giving the bill support from both parties, though it was never scheduled for action.

industries.note: The bill adds criminal jail time for intentional robocall violations and doubles fines for spoofed caller ID, directly raising the price of running mass calling scams.

Firms that follow the rules face no new penalties, but large-volume dialing operations bear new liability risk if they cross the 100,000-calls-per-day thresholds, so compliance costs rise slightly for the biggest players.
